title: ⭐⭐ Revision: from the circle to the appeal

questions.prompt: A charity buys a full page: a photograph of a crowded classroom, a sum printed larger than anything else on the sheet, a short paragraph of figures beneath it and a web address at the foot. A pupil says the page was made to inform its readers about a problem. What has he missed about it?

options.text: the page was written to teach its readers how school years are numbered
the page was written to answer something published about the charity
the page was bought to advertise a book about children out of school
every part of the page is aimed at getting money out of the reader

questions.explanation: Facts are certainly on that sheet, but they are not what it is for; they are the means. The sum stops the eye and makes the gift look small, the figures beneath it justify the sum, the photograph puts a face where the numbers were, and the address at the foot exists so that a reader who has been moved knows where to send something. A page that only wanted its readers better informed would have needed none of that machinery, and it would certainly not have ended on the one line that tells you where to pay. Nothing here is being sold, and nothing is being defended against anybody.

questions.prompt: Four sentences have been written about the same repair to a school roof. Three of them promise the same thing. Which is the odd sentence out?

options.text: Unless the roof is mended, the top classroom will stay shut.
If the roof is mended, the top classroom will stay shut.
If the roof is not mended, the top classroom will stay shut.
The top classroom will stay shut unless the roof is mended.

questions.explanation: Three of these sentences make the repair the way out: mend the roof and the room opens again. Two of them say so with a word that carries its own negative, once at the front of the sentence and once in the middle, which changes nothing but the order of the halves; the third says it with a plain negative behind if, which is the same trade written out longhand. One sentence alone puts a positive verb behind if, and that single change turns the promise upside down: it now says that mending the roof is what keeps the room shut, which is not a warning any head teacher would pin to a door.

questions.prompt: UNESCO and OPEC are both acronyms. What makes a set of letters an acronym?

options.text: each letter stands for one whole word of a name, taken in order
it is one long word with its middle and its ending cut off
it is a short label a body picks because it is easy to say
it is the mark of a body that belongs to the United Nations

questions.explanation: The machine is strict, and its strictness is what makes it useful: one letter, one word, and the words in the order the name has them, which is how a reader who has never met the letters before can unfold them. A word with its tail cut off is a different device and keeps its own name - a shortening, like Prof. for professor, where nothing stands for anything. Ease of pronunciation is a happy accident and no part of the rule. And membership decides nothing at all here: three of the bodies in this lesson are United Nations bodies and the rest are not, yet the letters of a fund for oil producers are built exactly the same way as the letters of the children's fund.

questions.prompt: A ministry wants to work with several neighbouring countries on a shared plan for training teachers and improving the way science is taught. Which of the two international bodies that deal with education should it write to, and on what ground?

options.text: UNICEF, whose business is children, and a teaching plan is written for children
UNESCO, whose business is providing schools with a meal in the middle of the day
UNESCO, whose business is educational and scientific cooperation between nations
UNICEF, which was founded in 1945 and is therefore the older of the two bodies

questions.explanation: Unfold the letters and the answer is nearly written for you: the body founded in 1945 has education, science and culture in its very name, and it was created to bring nations together through exactly those things. A plan shared between neighbouring ministries for their teachers and their laboratories is that work and nothing else. The children's fund does invaluable things for children, schooling among them, but it works for the child rather than for a joint programme between states. Two of these answers also carry a plain error of fact: feeding a school at midday is the food programme's task, not this body's, and it was the children's fund that was set up in 1946, a year later.

questions.prompt: A report counts 115 million children as being out of school. Which children does that phrase count?

options.text: children who have gone home for the evening and closed their books
children of school age whose names are on no register anywhere
children a teacher has sent to stand in the corridor for an hour
children who have finished their schooling and gone out to work

questions.explanation: The phrase looks as if it described where a child is standing at a given moment, and it does not: it describes a child's relation to the school system as a whole. Being counted here means that no school anywhere holds your name, either because none ever took you or because one has lost you. That is why the study these figures come from calls it exclusion, and why it can be measured once a year rather than at four o'clock. A child at home for the evening, a child punished in a corridor and a young worker who has finished are all outside a classroom at that instant, and not one of them is in this count.

questions.prompt: Four lines of the 2001/02 table, out of a world total of 115 million children out of school. West and Central Africa: 24.0 million. East Asia and the Pacific: 8.7 %. Latin America and the Caribbean: 3.3 million. Middle East and North Africa: 7.6 %. Put the four regions in order, from the one with the most children out of school to the one with the fewest.

options.text: West and Central Africa
East Asia and the Pacific
Latin America and the Caribbean
Middle East and North Africa

questions.explanation: Two lines give a head count and two give a share, so nothing can be compared until they are all in the same unit. Take the world total and read the shares off it: 8.7 per cent of 115 million is 10.0 million for the Pacific side of Asia, and 7.6 per cent comes out at 8.7 million for the Middle East and North Africa - the report prints 8.8 on that line, because the share it prints has itself been rounded before you ever multiply by it, and one tenth of one per cent of 115 million is more than a hundred thousand children. Either figure leaves the order untouched. The western and central belt of Africa is far ahead with 24.0 million, more than twice the next; then the ten million; then the Middle East and North Africa, close behind but never overtaking it; and Latin America with the Caribbean comes last on 3.3 million, barely a seventh of the leading figure. Comparing 8.7 with 24.0 as though both were the same kind of number is the one thing this table punishes.
